part.text: {"reframes":[{"bottleneck":"The ~25% floor is stated for absolute per-molecule properties, so the 8→24→48→120 ladder mostly re-measures the same floor with more precision; the quantity the pipeline actually needs — which of two candidates ranks higher — is never measured directly.","assumption":"That ranking accuracy is capped by absolute accuracy, i.e. that force-field errors are independent across molecules. Same-chemistry molecules share the same parameter bias, so errors are correlated and largely cancel inside a difference.","reframe":"Change the objective and the unit of work: from the absolute property of one molecule to the sign of the difference within a pair. Score pairwise ordering accuracy and spend simulation only on pairs the current ranking leaves ambiguous.","question":"For molecule pairs whose measured viscosities differ by at least 10%, what fraction are ordered the same way by the published Green–Kubo runs — and does that fraction stay at or above 0.9 while absolute per-molecule error stays near 25%?","measure":"Re-score the published 8-molecule table as 28 pairs (sign agreement for viscosity and for thermal conductivity); no new simulation, roughly an afternoon of analysis, under $10. If too few pairs clear the 10% separation, add the next 16 molecules (about $125 at the plan's ~$7.8 per molecule) and repeat.","compute_after":"If sign accuracy is high, the 120-molecule absolute-error campaign and the 15% error target can be dropped; compute moves to targeted paired runs near decision boundaries, with many candidate pairs run side by side.","exact":"fraction f of pairs (A,B) with |eta_meas(A)-eta_meas(B)|/eta_meas >= 0.10 for which sign[eta_MD(A)-eta_MD(B)] = sign[eta_meas(A)-eta_meas(B)]; the same quantity for thermal conductivity.","expected":"f >= 0.9 for both properties despite ~25% absolute error, because the shared chemistry bias appears in both members of a pair and cancels in the difference.","fails_if":"f <= 0.7, meaning the error is dominated by molecule-specific, uncorrelated noise; differences then inherit the full floor and ranking really is capped — the reframe buys nothing.","closest_prior":"The published 8-molecule benchmark [s_ogbomo_md] reports only per-molecule absolute errors; this re-scores the identical data as 28 pairwise decisions — beyond it at zero simulation cost."},{"bottleneck":"With LOPLS-AA parameters fixed, no amount of Green–Kubo sampling lowers the error floor: molecules 9–120 only estimate the same floor more precisely. The published result that all eight thermal conductivities are over-predicted points to a shared, parameter-level bias rather than random per-molecule error.","assumption":"That the force field is an untouchable input and error can only be corrected after the fact (the plan's output bias correction). The floor is treated as a fact of nature instead of as one or two mis-set parameters.","reframe":"Change the order of steps: before adding molecules, make the force field itself the object of compute — a small scaling sweep of the one or two Lennard-Jones or charge parameters plausibly carrying the bias, fit on the 8 known molecules, frozen, then tested on the next 8.","question":"Does a single global rescaling of one parameter class (for example the ester carbonyl LJ epsilon, or the united-atom CHx epsilon), fit to the 8 published viscosities, cut held-out viscosity error on 8 unseen molecules below 15%?","measure":"Kill-signal sweep: 5 epsilon-scale values x 8 molecules x one 2-ns run each = 80 ns, about $25 at the plan's ~$0.26/ns. Only if training error collapses monotonically, run the frozen setting on 8 new molecules with the full 6x5 ns protocol (240 ns, about $65). Total about $90.","compute_after":"If the refit transfers, compute buys depth instead of breadth: per-chemistry-class refits, then a corrected-field screen of the full 835-molecule set at a lower floor — more compute now changes the answer rather than re-measuring it.","exact":"held-out mean absolute percent error of Green–Kubo viscosity at 40 °C on 8 molecules excluded from the fit, using one frozen global scaling; secondary: the same for thermal conductivity.","expected":"Because all 8 conductivities were over-predicted (one shared sign), a single knob removes most of the bias; held-out viscosity error lands at 12–18%.","fails_if":"Best-fit training error stays above 20%, or the optimal scaling reverses sign between hydrocarbons and esters — then the error is molecule-specific, not parameter-level, and refitting merely overfits the eight.","closest_prior":"The published benchmark [s_ogbomo_md] holds the field fixed and only reports the bias; the plan corrects outputs afterward. Fitting the field against the same measurements is the step beyond both."},{"bottleneck":"The unit of work is a pure liquid, but the pipeline's product is a formulated single-phase coolant, usually a blend; the plan itself concedes it cannot show blends, so no amount of pure-molecule compute at 40 °C answers whether blend rankings are right.","assumption":"That pure-component rankings transfer to blends through an implicit mixing rule — that mixing adds no new error beyond the per-component floor.","reframe":"Change the unit of work from molecule to mixture: simulate the blend directly at several compositions, so compute acts on the object actually being ranked and measures whether mixing itself is predictable.","question":"For one binary pair from the benchmark set at three compositions (25/50/75 mol%), does direct blend simulation reproduce the measured blend viscosity within the same error band as the pure components, and does a mole-fraction mixing rule built from the already-simulated pures do measurably worse?","measure":"3 compositions x 6 replicas x 5 ns = 90 ns, about $25, using published blend data for the same pair; compare direct-blend error against the mixing-rule prediction from the existing pure simulations. Total about $25–50.","compute_after":"If direct-blend error tracks the pure-component floor, the search space opens up: compute screens blend compositions of a few validated components (combinatorially many liquids from few chemistries), and pure-molecule runs shrink to calibration.","exact":"mean absolute percent error versus measurement of Green–Kubo blend viscosity at 40 °C at mole fractions 0.25/0.50/0.75, compared against the mixing-rule prediction built from the two pure simulations.","expected":"Direct-blend error within roughly 5 points of the pure-component floor; the mixing rule biased by more than that for ester–hydrocarbon pairs, so direct simulation wins on ranking.","fails_if":"Blend error exceeds the pure floor by more than a factor of 2, or the ordering across compositions is wrong while pure ordering is right — blend MD then carries its own uncharacterized error that must be fixed before the reframe is usable.","closest_prior":"The 8-molecule pure-liquid benchmark and the 835-molecule reference set [s_ogbomo_md, s_ogbomo_db] contain no mixtures; even one binary composition series is beyond both."}]}
